name: Chlorine dioxide rinse

lead: A chlorine dioxide rinse is an alcohol-free mouthwash containing stabilized chlorine dioxide, sold to reduce bad breath. Breath-focused users like that it acts chemically on odor compounds rather than just masking them.

Chlorine dioxide is an oxidizer, and the proposed mechanism is oxidation of the volatile sulfur compounds that oral bacteria produce. An 8-week randomized, placebo-controlled trial tested it in people with intrinsic oral malodor, and Wikipedia cites a meta-analysis reporting benefit for halitosis.

paras: It is used as a regular rinse after tooth brushing, often as part of a broader breath routine with tongue cleaning. People tend to use it daily over several weeks.

Dilute oral rinsing is accepted in mouthwash use, but concentrated chlorine dioxide is toxic. The FDA warns against ingesting chlorine-dioxide products marketed as cures, which have caused serious injury; these are a different product from the mouthwash.

angle.text: Chlorine dioxide rinses are used by people targeting bad breath, since the oxidizer breaks down the volatile sulfur compounds responsible. A small randomized trial base exists for breath, and the mouthwash is a different product from toxic chlorine-dioxide cure products.

lead: A chlorine dioxide rinse is an alcohol-free mouthwash whose active ingredient is stabilized chlorine dioxide, an oxidizing agent. People use it for fresher breath, which matters for close-range social and dating situations, and proponents say it works by chemically neutralizing the volatile sulfur compounds (VSCs) responsible for much of oral odor rather than covering them with flavor [1].

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial published in 2018 tested an unflavored, non-fluoridated, alcohol-free stabilized chlorine dioxide mouthwash over eight weeks in healthy people with clinically diagnosed intrinsic oral malodor, as an adjunct to tooth brushing [1]. Wikipedia notes that dilute chlorine dioxide is an antiseptic ingredient in some mouthwashes and cites a meta-analysis reporting that daily use is linked to improved halitosis [2].

Chlorine dioxide is also a toxic industrial chemical, and the US Food and Drug Administration has warned against ingesting chlorine dioxide products marketed as cures, a different use from dilute oral rinsing.

paras: Chlorine dioxide is a strong oxidizer. Manufacturers and proponents describe the rinse as oxidizing odor-causing volatile sulfur compounds rather than simply masking them with flavoring [1]. The 2018 trial used an unflavored formulation versus a placebo rinse, which tested the active ingredient rather than flavor effects [1].

Most genuine bad breath begins in the mouth, where bacteria on the back of the tongue produce foul-smelling compounds including hydrogen sulfide and methyl mercaptan; gum disease, decay and trapped food also contribute [3]. Many mouthwashes target the anaerobic bacteria that release these compounds, and alcohol-based rinses can dry the mouth, which may favor those bacteria [2].

Mouthwashes for halitosis commonly contain cetylpyridinium chloride, chlorhexidine, zinc salts, hydrogen peroxide or chlorine dioxide [3]. Wikipedia's halitosis article says only chlorhexidine and cetylpyridinium chloride have tentative evidence of benefit and gives no evidence specific to chlorine dioxide or zinc, while the mouthwash article cites a 2023 meta-analysis linking daily chlorine dioxide rinse use to improved halitosis [2][3]. Cetylpyridinium chloride and chlorhexidine can temporarily stain teeth [2][3].

At the dilute concentrations used in mouthwash, chlorine dioxide is considered an acceptable antiseptic ingredient, according to Wikipedia's summary. The compound in concentrated or gaseous form is toxic and can decompose explosively, so it is normally handled as a dilute aqueous solution.

The FDA has stated that internal use of chlorine dioxide products has no health benefits, with dilute supervised oral rinsing as the exception, and has issued warnings about products such as Miracle Mineral Solution. Fraudulent marketing of chlorine dioxide as a cure for conditions including autism and COVID-19 has led to documented serious harm. These products are distinct from commercial mouthwashes.

An 8-week, single-site, two-way crossover randomized controlled trial compared a stabilized chlorine dioxide mouthwash with a placebo mouthwash as an adjunct to brushing in healthy subjects with clinically diagnosed intrinsic oral malodor [1]. Wikipedia cites meta-analyses reporting that daily use of chlorine dioxide rinse is associated with improved halitosis [2]. The body of published trials is small, and results are specific to the products tested.
